The Scalyfin weakfish Cynoscion squamipinnis is a sciaenid species for which detailed life-history data are gradually emerging from comparative studies with congeners. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been estimated at 3% [GSI = 3%] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Field surveys of adult Scalyfin weakfish indicate that the ultimate total length individuals can attain is approximately 64 centimeters [Li = approximately 64 centimeters], placing this species among the larger members of the genus. This maximum size is achieved only after several years of sustained somatic growth, which is closely tied to the local productivity of the estuarine habitats the species frequents throughout its range.

At the onset of sexual maturation, female Scalyfin weakfish typically reach a total length of roughly 30 centimeters [Lp = roughly 30 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the beginning of reproductive capacity. Corresponding to this length at puberty, the wet weight at puberty for females has been calculated from length-weight regressions at approximately 251 grams [Wwp = approximately 251 grams], a body mass that must be attained before vitellogenesis and oocyte development can proceed efficiently. This weight gain from the earliest life stages is considerable, given that the wet weight at birth following eclosion is a mere 0.0001 grams [Wwb = 0.0001 grams], a mass derived from the small, transparent, pelagic eggs that are typical of sciaenids. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva thus begins its life with extremely limited endogenous reserves, relying on the rapid absorption of yolk nutrients to transition quickly to exogenous feeding.

In contrast to the modest size at hatching, older adults can reach a substantial ultimate wet weight of 2554 grams [Wwi = 2554 grams], based on length-weight relationships established for the species. This represents an enormous increase in somatic mass from the larval stage, driven by a prolonged period of rapid mass gain during the juvenile and sub-adult phases. The shift from a planktonic larval existence to a demersal juvenile lifestyle is accompanied by dramatic allometric shifts and fin ray ossification, all of which support the eventual attainment of this large adult body size. The species' longevity, meanwhile, has been documented to extend for approximately seven years [am = approximately seven years] when assessed in populations inhabiting warm-temperate waters, though this lifespan is conditional upon the prevailing at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]thermal regime. For populations experiencing a sustained environmental temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan aligns closely with this seven-year estimate, a duration that permits multiple reproductive seasons for iteroparous females.

The gonadosomatic index of 3% [GSI = 3%] was recorded at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This pattern is consistent with a batch-spawning strategy, where multiple spawning events occur over an extended season, rather than a single, massive investment of somatic resources into a single clutch. The moderate length at puberty of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters] ensures that females can begin contributing to the population at a size that is still below the peak predatory pressure from larger piscivores. Conversely, the ultimate total length of 64 centimeters [Li = 64 centimeters] likely represents the size at which individuals can avoid most gape-limited predators, thereby reducing natural mortality among the oldest and largest members of the population.

Comparative studies with other sciaenids reveal that the lifespan of Cynoscion squamipinnis is relatively extended for a species of its body size, with the oldest individuals reaching an age of seven years [am = seven years] in their natural habitat at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This longevity is closely linked to the thermal conditions of the species' environment, as metabolic rates and senescence are strongly temperature-dependent; at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the pace of life is accelerated compared to cooler-water congeners, yet the species still manages to achieve a substantial adult mass. The ultimate wet weight of 2554 grams [Wwi = 2554 grams] is among the highest recorded for weakfish in the eastern Pacific, reflecting both the favorable growing conditions and the efficient foraging ecology of adults. The rapid growth trajectory from the minuscule 0.0001 gram [Wwb = 0.0001 gram] birth mass to the 251 gram [Wwp = 251 gram] puberty threshold spans several years and involves dramatic ecological shifts — from pelagic larva to benthic juvenile to piscivorous adult — with each transition requiring specific habitat conditions and prey availability for successful recruitment into the next life stage.
